implementation_notes: The platform container plays the injector: register interface-to-implementation mappings (or factories) on the IServiceCollection while building the host, then let the container call constructors whose parameters are the registered services - IServiceProvider is the resolver and IHost.Services exposes it in hosted apps. What replaces the classic hand-written assembler is this registration list plus the lifetime methods (AddTransient/AddScoped/AddSingleton), while the consumer stays a plain class with constructor parameters. The host validates only what it is told to (ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild in development), so lifetime mistakes - a singleton holding a scoped service - are the pitfall to watch.
pitfalls: Captive dependency: resolving a scoped service from a singleton makes it live for the process lifetime - enable ValidateScopes and check lifetimes.
Service locator in disguise: injecting IServiceProvider (or using app.Services in handlers) hides dependencies and defeats the pattern.
Multiple registrations: GetService returns the last registration while GetServices returns all - ambiguity is silent.

variants.name: Hand-wired composition root without a container
variants.idiom_name: plain constructors called from one composition root
variants.implementation_notes: Before and instead of the container, a C# app can wire everything by hand: build the graph in Program.Main or a small factory class, pass interfaces into constructors, and keep lifetimes as ordinary C# scopes (using/await using, IDisposable). This is the right default for libraries, console tools and small services, and it is exactly what the container automates once the graph or the lifetime matrix outgrows a screenful. Mixing the two is common: hand-wire the leaves (options, HttpClient) and register the rest.
pitfalls: Disposal becomes manual: whoever owns the graph must dispose IDisposable leaves (using/await using), where the container would do it.
Rebuilding the graph per request accidentally creates duplicate clients and pools; hold the root's instances deliberately.
